authored.title: Khun Phaen (the hero inside the amulet)
authored.body_html:
What this is

Khun Phaen (ขุนแผน) is the hero of the Thai epic Khun Chang Khun Phaen — soldier, seducer, and master of the wichaa — and the only figure in this archive who is at once a literary character, an invoked teacher, a family of na, katha, and yant, and one of the most-traded amulet classes on the living market. Most subjects here are a text-type or a being; Khun Phaen is a person the tradition kept using after his story ended. This page tells enough of the story to make the objects legible, then follows him through the printed treatises the corpus holds and out onto the market that still trades under his name — where he turns out to be the single most instructive object in the whole amulet taxonomy: a pressed tablet in Buddha-amulet form made with prai-kuman material, a hybrid whose two halves are both, as it happens, in the epic.

The story, first

Tradition holds — the epic ran for centuries as oral sepha recitation, performers rapping krap sticks in market squares and temple fairs, before the Bangkok court fixed it in print. It begins with an execution: the boy Phlai Kaeo's father, a royal officer, botches a buffalo roundup and is put to death by the king, and the family scatters. The fatherless boy ordains as a novice — and turns out to be brilliant at exactly the curriculum this archive catalogues. In the monasteries of Suphanburi and Kanchanaburi he learns invulnerability, invisibility, love-charms, and the raising of spirits; his teacher Ajarn Khong of Wat Khae is remembered for lessons like enchanting tamarind leaves into wasps — the temple still shows visitors the tamarind tree. Note what the epic has done here: the greatest magician in Thai literature is monastery-made. His power wears a monk's form from the first page.

Tradition holds — the rest of his life runs on the two engines the amulets still advertise, เสน่ห์ and คงกระพัน — charm and invulnerability. Still a novice, he wins Phim Philalai (later renamed Wanthong) at a Songkran festival; summoned to war on his wedding night, he returns victorious from the north to find his rich, bald rival Khun Chang has faked his death and married her. The epic's most famous night-scene is a working demonstration of this page's subject matter: Khun Phaen enters Khun Chang's compound with charms that put the whole household into enchanted sleep, walks room by room past the guards, and carries Wanthong off on horseback into the forest — where they live as fugitives while the kingdom hunts them. Readers have always noticed the moral weather of this: the same man is the epic's most devout and its most dangerous, and the poem never resolves the tension. Neither do the amulets.

Tradition holds — the Golden Boy is made in the darkest of these fugitive years. Bua Khli, a bandit chief's daughter Khun Phaen has married on the run, is ordered by her father to poison him; warned in time, he cuts his unborn son from her body, carries the child to the ordination hall of a temple, and roasts him over a fire through the night, chanting, while the hall's consecrated boundary holds every rival spirit out — until at dawn the boy's spirit speaks, and serves his father ever after as scout, sentry, and spy. This is the origin story the kuman-thong practice cites for itself, and the scene the amulet trade never forgot: when a modern maker presses prai-kuman powder into a tablet stamped with Khun Phaen's name, this night is the warrant.

Tradition holds — the epic does not end in his triumph. It ends with the king demanding that Wanthong choose at last between her two men; she stands silent — the poem lets her be the only honest person at court — and is executed for it, her son's royal pardon arriving minutes too late. The hero outlives everyone he charmed. That, too, is in the amulets: nothing about Khun Phaen's magic promises a happy ending — it promises effect.

Two facts from all this do the work below: his magic is monastery-trained, Buddhist in form; and the kuman thong is his making. Form and material, already assigned.

The market walk — ชมตลาด

Tradition holds — the name ขุนแผนชมตลาด, "Khun Phaen admires the market," remembers the hero strolling a market street with every head turning as he passes — admiring, and admired. The corpus carries the katha itself, in plain first-person Thai rather than Pali (vedic-katha-for-chai-chatri p.90–91), and it is a strut set to a drumbeat: "Om, may I succeed! …my glory is as beautiful as the sky, my arms as beautiful as Narayana's, my radiance the sun's, my power the moon's; not one maiden in the heavenly city can help but long for my face." Then the boast climbs a ladder of similes, each rung punctuated นะ มะ พะ ทะ: may they be dazed as the swan-king who swallowed water and lost himself; as the great fish who forgot Mother Ganges; may kings forget their thrones and beds, the servant girl forget her mistress, the old woman fall in love, the devout man forget his prayers — and "the young hen abandon her chicks and come running after me," the kai making its cameo in another bird's register. After all that thunder, the instructions are a cosmetics counter: chant it over face powder, perfumed hair-oil, lip-wax; it works "both toward noble patrons and toward women." A war-god's speech, deployed via makeup.

The same name attaches to a drawn na. The Scripture of 108 Magical Na gives นะขุนแผนชมตลาด twice (scripture-of-108-magical-na p.13, p.43 — one copy credited to Wat Samrong), and its inscription formula is its own best gloss: the na is built in six recited steps — first, the princess; second, the prince; third, a woman; fourth, a man; fifth, a female merchant; sixth, a male merchant — the market crowd assembled person by person into the glyph before it is consecrated for "loving-favor from all people." Inference — the sutra answers the question the name poses: what does Khun Phaen see when he admires the market? Everyone in it, one by one, and the na holds them all.

The soldier's half

The love-charm is only half the repertoire; the epic's Khun Phaen is a soldier, and his corpus keeps the soldier's tools — with the epic itself cited as the case record.

The best story in the set is the invisibility katha (vedic-katha-for-chai-chatri p.86), whose instructions read like a fugitive's field manual, because that is what they are. Sit — leaning against a tree is fine — with your feet drawn in to close the body's openings, and recite without letting the words drop: no one will see you. If several pursuers are closing in, the treatise offers the most audacious sentence in the corpus: have your companions sit stacked one on top of another, and ride on top of the stack — the whole tower is shielded. Traveling by boat, consecrate three sprigs of the "leaf that knows how to sleep" and fix them at bow, midship, and stern; you will glide past the customs post unchallenged. And then the treatise names its authority — not a monk, but the poem: "in the story of Khun Chang Khun Phaen, this very katha was used, consecrating a hing leaf to blind pursuers' eyes all the way to Chiang Mai." The epic is cited the way a law report cites precedent: it worked for the fugitive in the tale; it will work for you.

  • นะขุนแผน (นะกำบัง) — the Concealment Na (scripture-of-108-magical-na p.51, credited to Luang Pu Chaeng) runs the same logic in drawn form: each stroke of the five-step inscription is paired with a hiding — na wards, mo closes, phut hides completely, tha surrounds the body, ya hides the head.
  • พระคาถามหาชาตรีขุนแผน — the Great Warrior katha (vedic-katha-for-chai-chatri p.81–82): a long syllable-string chanted over food, liquor, or sesame oil for invulnerability, with a testing protocol included — "try hacking at it with an axe; the blade can do no harm at all" — and a plain attribution: "it is a katha of Khun Phaen."
  • หัวใจขุนแผน — the whole man compressed to four syllables, สุนะโมโล (biography-of-lp-thob-and-his-katha p.104): chant it over the clothes you wear, for popularity. The same four syllables sit in the mnemonic curriculum tables of two separate treatises (vedic-katha-for-chai-chatri p.50; yantra-inscription-formulas-khom-thai p.20), filed between the Yaksha King and the Diamond Armor — Khun Phaen as a standard entry in the syllable canon, alongside suttas and gods.

A further na-index page (scripture-of-108-magical-na p.96) shows นะขุนแผน as one glyph in a gallery of twenty-five named na — between the Tiger and the World-Devastator — each a little machine of zigzags, loops, and spiral coils. Whatever else he is, in these books Khun Phaen is a repertoire slot: a name a na, a katha, a heart-syllable, and a yant can each be filed under.

Worn, inked, and held

  • ยันต์สาริกาลิ้นทองขุนแผน — the Golden-Tongued Mynah of Khun Phaen (yantra-inscription-formulas-khom-thai p.55): a teardrop yant inscribed on a takrut and worn in the mouth, consecrated 108 times — sweet speech, carried at the point of speech, for a hero whose voice talked its way into guarded houses.
  • นะขุนแผนมหาเสน่ห์ — a sak-yant stencil (sak-yant-stencils-for-tracing): two five-spired pagoda-shaped charts of Khom syllables, ready to trace onto skin. The na has left the paper for the body.
  • The verse "used with a Phra Khun Phaen" (biography-of-lp-thob-and-his-katha p.102) comes wrapped in its own initiation drama. To learn it at all, the teacher requires a formal homage-rite — five kinds of flowers, five candles, five incense sticks, begun on a Thursday. Then chant it over lip-wax or face powder — it has a slot where you say the beloved's name — and use it "together with a Khun Phaen amulet, to excellent effect." Printed right beneath: the teachers forbid passing this knowledge on, "trust this and never violate it." This is the bridge sentence of the whole page: the printed katha reaches out and touches the market object, and the object is expected to be there.
  • The powder and the held image (mind-stream-key-to-saiyasat p.110–111) is a story told in the first person. A master dreams an instruction: gather the flowers monks offer each other at the rite of mutual forgiveness before the Rains Retreat — from 108 temples in a single day — with moss from a relic stupa and from a sacred Bodhi tree, and press Buddha images from them. He wakes joyful, sends word to disciples across every province, and among the relics that come back is one he names with a straight face: "the special powder of Ajarn Khong, teacher of Khun Phaen," dug from beneath a stupa in Si Prachan district, Suphanburi — the epic's home ground yielding physical provenance for a literary teacher, complete with its own history attached. The method of use that follows: hold the image in the hand, breathe phut in and tho out until the mind settles, then recite "remembering Ajarn Khong and Ajarn Khun Phaen" until the deva comes down to possess the medium. Inference — the treatises handle Khun Phaen precisely as they handle historical masters: his teacher leaves relics, his name is called in invocation, his lineage warrants powder. Whether he "existed" is not a question the shelf asks.

A Buddha's form, a kuman's material

On the living market the hybrid is measurable. Of the 13,020 amulet listings in the market layer's Lazada snapshot, 237 name ขุนแผน in the title. The classic form is a pressed tablet showing a seated Buddha — form phra khrueang, indistinguishable at arm's length from any votive amulet — but the material tells the other half: 126 of the 237 mention phrai in some form, 101 say ผงพราย (prai powder) outright, 91 say พรายกุมาร, and 67 claim kru (excavated-cache) provenance. The effect vocabulary is the chom-talat katha's own: เมตตา (71), เสน่ห์ (63), มหานิยม (38), ค้าขาย (14) — and three listings sell a รุ่น named ชมตลาด, the manuscript katha's title running as a current product name. Prices sit low and lively: the middle half of the market runs ฿84–257, median ฿173, and the 95 listings that report sales have moved some 8,700 units between them. This is a folk hero with distribution.

The taxonomy note in the archive's own class vocabulary reads the seam carefully: of 389 listings naming กุมาร at all, 106 are Khun Phaen — and those 106 must not be read as free-standing kuman, dolls to raise and feed. The Khun Phaen is a true hybrid: Buddha-amulet form, prai-kuman material — the upkeep of an amulet, the provenance-sensitivity of prai. A scanner that tags it "kuman" because the word is present is honest about the word and wrong about the object. Inference — the hybrid is the epic compressed to a pressed tablet: the man trained in the monastery (the Buddha's form, outside) who roasted his son into a servant-spirit (the kuman's material, within). The amulet is his biography in cross-section.

The market keeps drifting the form toward the story, too: sixteen listings are ขุนแผนอุ้มนาง — Khun Phaen holding the maiden — the tablet giving up the Buddha-image altogether and pressing the epic scene itself, the horseback abduction from Khun Chang's house rendered at pendant scale. And the reference treatise's entry for the class (the bilingual charm treatise, entry A·04) files him as "charm of the irresistible warrior," a moulded tablet from the Ayutthaya epic "often carrying a Plai Kuman guardian spirit," and names the line collectors name first: ขุนแผนพลายกุมาร of Luang Pho Kuay, Wat Khositaram (Chainat).

What the catalogue holds

Search the palm-leaf catalogue and it goes silent: ขุนแผน scores zero across all 6,990 titles — as does ขุนช้าง. Every witness on this page is a contributed printed treatise from a Central Thai press. The silence has two readings, and both are probably true. First, the lesson the paṭiloma page already taught: this register lives at section level, inside untitled ยันต์-and-คาถา compendia a title search cannot see — a นะขุนแผน may well be waiting, unindexed, in a Nan or Lampang bundle. Second, the geography: the epic is Ayutthaya's and Suphanburi's, and in it Chiang Mai is the other side — the campaign's far city, the enemy capital the hero rides against. Inference — the Lanna shelf kept its own heroes and let the lowland keep this one; yet the epic itself knew the road north — its fugitives flee to Chiang Mai, hing leaf in hand — and the printed treatises that carry his katha circulated everywhere. A close read of the northern compendia, not a title search, is what would settle where Khun Phaen's wichaa actually traveled.

Notes

  • Read alongside katha and yantra. Khun Phaen is a name that organizes instances of both; those pages hold the corpus counts for the forms themselves.
  • The market layer is the living half of this page. The products widget and prices widget draw from the same snapshot the numbers above come from; the 237-listing slice is a data-aggregation surface, not a storefront.
  • A crawl and transcription priority. Any fresh transcription of an untitled yant-and-katha bundle from the northern provinces is a chance to find the na-repertoire — ขุนแผน included — under Lanna hands. The six printed witnesses here give the search image: look for the six-step chom-talat inscription, the สุนะโมโล heart-syllable, and the concealment pairing.
